from pathlib import Path

 out.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n\\n'+t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(out))
print(''.join(out)[:42000])

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant limitation of classifier-based Bayesian optimization: repeated exploitation of regions already judged promising. Incorporating unlabeled candidate geometry through label propagation and label spreading is a useful combination of established methods, particularly for fixed candidate pools.

The empirical study compares against GP-EI/UCB and multiple BORE/LFBO classifiers across synthetic, hyperparameter optimization, neural architecture search, and image-based tasks. Twenty repetitions with standard errors provide meaningful evidence of improvements, especially on the synthetic and NATS-Bench experiments.

The pseudocode and supplementary studies make the approach broadly understandable. Ablations cover kernel bandwidth, unlabeled sample count, sampling distribution, pool subsampling, and threshold ratio; the paper also acknowledges computational limitations and cases where GP baselines perform better.
weaknesses: The central attribution to semi-supervised learning is insufficiently established. Figure 12 includes a valuable no-unlabeled-data baseline, but it sometimes outperforms the proposed variants, notably on Bukin6 and Branin. This ablation fixes β=0.5, whereas the main experiments learn substantially different bandwidths. Comparisons against a well-tuned supervised kernel classifier, with controlled bandwidth and randomized tie-breaking, are needed to isolate the contribution of unlabeled points. Random search and simple exploration-augmented BORE/LFBO would also help determine whether the gains require graph-based learning.

The cluster-assumption justification is not convincing. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated inputs does not ensure that points connected through high-density regions share the threshold-derived label, especially as the threshold changes during optimization. Appendix C explicitly acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. classification results do not apply to adaptive BO; it also does not establish the claimed expansion of the favorable decision region. Consequently, improved exploration remains a plausible explanation rather than a demonstrated mechanism.

Important implementation details remain unspecified: feature scaling, propagation parameters α/τ/ε, initialization and bounds for bandwidth optimization, acquisition maximization over arbitrary fixed pools, and handling of previously evaluated candidates. These choices directly affect graph geometry and optimization behavior. A smaller, correctable mathematical inconsistency also appears in Section 4.1: the scalar definition of p_ij is column-normalized, whereas P=D^-1W is row-normalized, making the intended propagation update ambiguous.

Evidence for general high-dimensional optimization is limited. All continuous synthetic functions are two-dimensional. The 64D MNIST experiment uses embeddings trained on 440,000 examples labeled with the same three-digit values being optimized. Although this representation is shared across methods, it supplies substantial objective-related information and favorable geometry; performance there does not establish robustness on generic high-dimensional black-box problems.

The practical computational tradeoff is inadequately quantified. Dense graph construction, repeated bandwidth optimization, and 1,000 acquisition-optimization restarts can be expensive. Appendix G measures sensitivity to pool size with fixed bandwidth, but provides no end-to-end runtime comparison against competitors under the main experimental settings. Thus, the sample-efficiency gains cannot yet be assessed against their computational cost.
